title: Unilateral Crosstalk Cancellation via Bone Conduction: Methods and Evaluation
author: Irwansyah, Otsuka, et al.

steps.title: Prepare participant and sensors
steps.instruction: Recruit seven normal‑hearing participants (5 M, 2 F, ages 21‑32), perform otoscopic examination, obtain written informed consent, fit each subject with audiometric bone transducers, place a probe microphone in the left ear canal and an accelerometer on the left mastoid as the target cancellation sites, and schedule testing sessions (≈1.5 h per sensor location) across two days.

steps.title: Estimate impulse responses
steps.instruction: Acquire the impulse responses of the bone‑conduction paths needed for later crosstalk‑compensation filter design.

steps.title: Estimate CTC filter
steps.instruction: Compute the crosstalk‑compensation (CTC) filter from the measured impulse responses using the adaptive algorithm described for low‑frequency zone‑of‑quiet generation.

steps.title: Verify CTC filter performance
steps.instruction: Assess the effectiveness of the CTC filter at the chosen sensor location (probe microphone or mastoid) by measuring residual sound levels to confirm creation of a zone of quiet.

steps.title: Measure thresholds with adaptive 3IFC
steps.instruction: Using a custom Python IPyWidgets GUI, run a 2‑down/1‑up three‑interval forced‑choice (3IFC) procedure for each test frequency and condition (with or without crosstalk cancellation): start the pure‑tone level at –20 dB re 1 V RMS, present three audio intervals (one contains the pure tone, all contain noise) and let the subject select the interval via a button; after two consecutive correct responses decrease the level by 4 dB, after an incorrect response increase by 4 dB; after four reversals reduce the step size to 2 dB; continue until a total of 12 reversals are obtained; calculate the threshold by averaging the intensity values of the last eight reversals; repeat for all frequencies tested.

steps.title: Conduct earplug depth occlusion test
steps.instruction: Evaluate three earplug insertion depths—shallow (~6 mm), mid‑depth (~12 mm), and deep (18–24 mm)—to quantify the occlusion effect: use the Resonance R17A‑BC audiometer with the same bone transducers, measure thresholds in the left ear while masking the right ear with a Radioear DD45 headset delivering narrow‑band noise (‑24 dB/oct slope) centred on the test frequency; test octave frequencies from 250 Hz to 4000 Hz starting at 1000 Hz; begin with a clearly audible tone (~30 dB), decrease intensity in 10 dB steps until inaudible, then increase in 5 dB steps until audible again, employing a bracketing procedure; record the lowest intensity detected in at least two of three presentations as the threshold; repeat the procedure for each earplug depth while keeping bone transducer positioning constant; each participant requires ≈20–30 min.

description: Although the “two-BT” technique has shown efficacy in reducing crosstalk within the frequency range of 1 kHz to 4 kHz, it encounters limitations when applied to frequencies below 1 kHz [11]. The sensitivity to phase differences between the cochleae in low-frequency pure tones creates ambiguity in the lateralization cues. This ambiguity complicates the task of phase and level adjustment by participants during sound lateralization tasks [11]. As a result, the utility of the “two-BT” method is essentially confined to frequencies above 1 kHz. Given the crucial role of localization cues at low frequencies [12], the development of a method capable of addressing crosstalk cancellation specifically for frequencies below 1 kHz is of utmost importance. In this paper, we detail a method for cancelling low-frequency crosstalk that takes advantage of the “zone of quiet” concept from active noise control (ANC) [13]. This method employs an adaptive algorithm to generate the necessary anti-signal for crosstalk cancellation at a strategically placed error sensor, thereby creating a zone of significantly reduced sound around the sensor. The size of this zone is frequency-dependant, with lower frequencies yielding larger zones. When the error sensor is positioned in proximity to the cochlea, such as within the ear canal or on the mastoid, the “zone of quiet” (depicted in Fig. 2) can extend to the cochlea within the inner ear, facilitating the effective cancellation of low-frequency crosstalk. By leveraging the “zone of quiet” concept, this method presents a potential improvement in crosstalk cancellation at low frequencies, where psychoacoustic-based methods like the “two-BT” method encounter limitations.Fig. 2Illustration of unilateral crosstalk cancellation: An accelerometer on the mastoid serves as the target cancellation site.
